newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy hard left willing to discuss pension reform.
newsitem.headline: Italy hard left willing to discuss pension reform.

text.p: Italy's hard-left Communist Refoundation (RC) is willing to discuss with the government some planned pension cuts and measures to make the social welfare system more efficient, Nerio Nesi, economic spokesman for the party told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).
"We agree with cuts in baby pensions and we agree with cuts in double or triple pensions," Nesi said in an interview.

Under Italy's pensions system some workers, dubbed baby pensioners, can retire after paying just 35 years of contributions. And many people draw retirement, disability, widows' and widowers' pensions all at the same time.
"We realise that it is necessary in some way to reduce social welfare spending, but we are talking about organisational expenditure and not a reduction in social services," he said.

The centre-left government of Prime Minister Romano Prodi announced last month it will soon implement a supplementary mini-budget to ensure Italy meets the 3.0 percent ratio between deficit and gross domestic product for early entry into the single European currency.
Prodi has said that most of these deficit-cutting measures of up to 14.6 trillion lire would be structural.
Refoundation, whose support is crucial in the lower house of parliament, has rigidly opposed any cuts in social spending or new taxes.

Asked how the government could win the support of RC with these conditions, Nesi said, "We want to protect the working class...but we don't want to protect the privileged. This is already a position which should be reassuring."

Nesi said Italy in the past had been much too generous over pension rights, particularly regarding the baby pensions. "Young people who went to work in a bank at 18 or 19 and then came out at 38-39 (with a pension). This is unacceptable."
Nesi said RC was urging the government to make a distinction between those who were privileged and those who were not, "and we'll be ready to discuss this."

Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti has met leading government figures in recent days to try to resolve deep differences between his party and the ruling coalition over the planned mini-budget, privatisations and reform of the welfare state.
